newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Impact of fresh Indonesian ethnic clash unclear.
newsitem.headline: Impact of fresh Indonesian ethnic clash unclear.

text.p: Indonesia's military said on Saturday the extent of casualties from fresh ethnic clashes in the country's West Kalimantan province was unclear, the Banjarmasin Post newspaper reported.

An army spokesman said fighting between local Dayak tribesmen and migrants from the island of Madura took place on Friday in the small village of Tebas, about 150 km (93 miles) north of the provincial capital of Pontianak.

Lieutenant-Colonel Sjachranuddin, spokesman for the regional military command covering the Indonesian half of Borneo island, was quoted by the paper in neighbouring South Kalimantan as saying people had been hurt in Tebas.

"There (are) certainly victims, but we do not know the amount for certain. Maybe they are just light injuries (or) serious injuries...rather than deaths. We still do not know for sure about the victims," he was quoted as saying on Saturday.
Police on Friday had been unable to give details of the renewed ethnic violence or declined to comment.
Church sources in Sambas, 20 km (12 miles) north of Tebas, said they had heard two people had been killed in Friday's clash and a number of buildings burnt but details remained sketchy.
The indigenous Dayaks are often Christian and the Madurese Moslem in mostly Islamic Indonesia, where various ethnic and religious riots have left at least 12 people dead since October.

Residents elsewhere in the province said on Friday tension remained high in Pontianak and the regional towns of Singkawang and Sanggau. Soldiers have blocked all key roads leading to the province's interior on Borneo Island for the past week.

Marzuki Darusman, deputy chairman of the official National Commission on Human Rights, told Reuters on Saturday the body was monitoring the situation but had not yet decided to send an investigation team to the area.

"We are not denying that things are still developing there but we think it is for the authorities to take care of them," Darusman said, adding the commission usually acted if the government was slow in intervening.
He said the commission would still investigate if it received reports of significant human rights abuses.

The tension, which residents say began in late December, exploded on New Year's Day when about 5,000 Dayak tribesmen rioted in Sanggau Ledo, 95 km (60 miles) north of Pontianak, attacking the Madurese. At least five died in the clashes.

Residents in Sanggau, 140 km (87 miles) east of Pontianak, said five Dayaks were killed last week when a crowd of about 200 Dayaks attacked a camp of more than 1,000 Madurese refugees guarded by soldiers.
The Madurese had fled to the town after earlier fighting.
